name: Caused-Motion Construction

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb followed by an NP direct object and an object-oriented locative PP complement
dimensions.meaning: The subject referent causes the direct-object referent to move along a path, from a source, toward a direction, or to a goal
dimensions.function: Packages a causing event and the resulting change of location; the verb can supply manner or causal means
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal in active and passive clauses; productive with verbs that do not lexically license the object or locative complement

1.definition: The subject participant causes the direct-object theme to undergo the change of location described by the locative complement
1.details: The construction, not necessarily the verb's lexical valency, licenses the theme object and locative complement. In He sneezed his tooth right across town, sneeze supplies the causal event while the frame supplies the caused-motion relation. In CGEL terms, across town is an object-oriented locative complement with a path/goal construal, not an adjunct, a predicative complement, or a second object of the verb (CGEL pp. 257–59, 684–88; Goldberg 2006: 6, 33–35, 94, 98–100).

examples.note: Attested Munsch/Goldberg example with a path/goal construal; sneeze does not independently have a three-argument sense
The verb supplies the means; the frame supplies caused motion and goal

constraints.description: The NP after the verb is Od; the following PP is an object-oriented locative complement, not a second object and not a locative adjunct.
The external subject must be construable as the source of causal force; volition is not required, as sneeze and knock show.

The direct-object referent is construed as the moving theme, and the PP supplies source, path, goal, or direction. Static caused-location uses require a separate extension and are not included in this core pattern.
The verbal event must be construable as causally relevant means or manner; productivity is constrained by semantic similarity and statistical pre-emption.

projection.target: Recognizing the Head–Od–locative-complement frame predicts a causer subject, a moving-theme object, an object-oriented change-of-location PP, and a caused-motion reading even when the verb does not lexically license those dependents
projection.evidence: Novel sneeze examples isolate constructional licensing (Goldberg 2006: 6, 94, 98–100); child-directed-speech results support predictive association between the form and caused-motion meaning (pp. 106–10); CGEL p. 684 treats change-of-location dependents as complements in motion frames

grounds.note: Productive licensing with non-motion verbs and form-meaning association
Productivity and learning evidence support a stable form-meaning profile

core.property: NP direct object as moving theme

diagnostics: source, path, goal, or direction interpretation
verb contributes manner or means rather than all valency

known_boundary_items: Caused location, enabled motion, and prevented motion are established extensions, but they do not replace the core caused-motion meaning.
CGEL calls the PP a locative complement and keeps locatives distinct from predicative complements; causative path resultative is a construction-family label, not the CGEL function label.

relatedConstructions.notes: Caused motion is a VP-level argument-structure specialization
The moving-theme direct object is normally realized by an NP
The final dependent is a locative PP complement
Transitive sister of the intransitive motion/goal frame; caused motion adds an Od theme
The final locative complement can bear the source role

grounds.note: The post-object PP is an object-oriented locative complement bearing a change-of-location role

curious.title: Making something move with a verb
curious.summary: A verb can be followed by a thing and a place phrase, showing that someone caused the thing to move.
curious.body:
In She sneezed the foam off the cappuccino, the sneeze makes the foam move. Sneeze doesn't have a sense with a moving thing and a path of its own, but the pattern supplies both.

Pat shoveled the hay into the wagon works the same way. The verb says how the causing happens, here shoveling, and the pattern adds the movement: someone makes something travel from a place, along a path, toward a direction or to a goal. The subject only has to be the source of the force. It doesn't have to act on purpose, as sneezing shows.
curious.try: Think of an action, like kicking or pushing. Can you say what it moved and where it went?

teacher.summary: Helps students see that some verbs get an object and a place phrase from the pattern itself, not from the verb alone.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb, a direct object noun phrase that is the moving theme, and a locative PP complement giving source, path, goal or direction. The subject causes the movement. The construction, not necessarily the verb, licenses the object and the PP: sneeze supplies the causing event, the frame supplies the caused motion. The PP is an object-oriented locative complement, not an adjunct, a predicative complement or a second object. The verb must be construable as the means or manner, and productivity is limited by semantic similarity.
teacher.terms: Caused-motion construction is the constructional name for the pattern. CGEL: the PP is an object-oriented locative complement. Od is the direct object.

contrasts.text: Pat shoveled the hay into the wagon.
contrasts.note: Direct object plus locative complement. The hay moves into the wagon.
Direct object only. There is no path phrase, so no caused-motion pattern.

watch_for: A learner might read into the wagon as a second object of the verb.
A learner might read the place phrase as a setting adjunct, when it describes where the object moves.
A learner might assume any verb can be used this way, when productivity depends on semantic similarity and on the verb's role as means or manner.
teacher.activity: Give students verbs such as sneeze, shovel and kick, plus a thing and a place. They build caused-motion sentences, then decide which show something moving from a source, along a path or to a goal.

child.hook: Can a sneeze send a tooth across town?
child.explain: Some sentences tell who made something move. Pat shoveled the hay into the wagon. Pat made the hay move, and the words into the wagon tell where the hay went.
child.play: Pick an action like kick, push or blow. Say what it moved and where it went. Can your friends guess the action?
